title: Wren and Puff's Sparkle Mission
markdown:
The valley looked as if it had been dipped in a giant sugar bowl, all sparkly white snow. Living there was a little robin named Wren. Cheerful, fluffing her feathers each morning, pecking at a seed, then singing the happiest songs you ever did hear. Her songs were so sunny they could almost make a little patch of snow giggle and melt.

Down below, snuggled in the warm cozy chimneys of the village houses, lived the cutest little chimney dragons. Small, no bigger than a yummy loaf of bread, scales shimmering like embers from a campfire. The favorite one was named Puff. Scales the color of a sleepy sunset, rosy pinks and warm oranges, and when he breathed out it smelled just like cinnamon toast. A gentle soul, usually found snoozing amongst the warm bricks, dreaming dragon dreams.

Every day, when the villagers woke and popped a fire in their hearth, something magical happened. The warm smoky breath from the chimneys did not just float away. It puffed out in little twinkly shapes, like tiny golden stars. They floated up past the pine trees wearing their snowy hats and into the big blue winter sky, joining the other smoke-stars, making the sky twinkle like a sleepy diamond necklace. Wren loved watching them.

“Hooray for smoke-stars.” She did a little happy loop-de-loop. The smoke-stars seemed to wink right back.

Until one day a peculiar chill, extra-icy and extra-shiver-worthy, snuck into the valley. A cold that made your nose hairs do a little dance and your toes feel like tiny ice cubes. The smoke-stars, instead of boogying up to the sky, started to wobble. They wiggled this way and that, then slowly, sadly, began to drift away from their chimneys, like lost little balloons caught in a whisper of wind. They looked so lonely. Their twinkles grew dim.

The village started to feel a little less sparkly. The sky, instead of a happy twinkle, looked a bit grey and droopy, like a giant grumpy cloud. The little cottages huddled closer together, as if for a warmth that was not quite there. Wren, usually bursting with songs, felt a tiny flutter in her chest, like a nervous butterfly doing cartwheels. Not really scary. A quiet worry. And Puff, who was supposed to be having his extra-long winter nap, felt a tickle in his smoky snout. He opened one sleepy golden eye, then the other.

“That’s odd.” Voice like a gentle puff of warm air. “The smoke-stars smell lonely. And a bit chilly.” He wiggled his little dragon tail, which for Puff was like a big wave of uh-oh.

Wren and Puff knew they had to do something. Wren, with super-fast wings and sharp eyes that could spot a crumb from a mile away, and Puff, with his gentle warm breath that smelled like happy memories of baking, were a very different pair. Wren could zip and zoom anywhere in a blink. Puff was like a tiny warm cloud of comfort and cinnamon. They decided to team up. Wren landed right on Puff’s head, tiny feet tickling his sunset-colored scales.

“Okay, Puff. We need to catch those wander-stars. They’re getting lost.”

They hatched a plan. A bit silly, but brilliant. Wren, perched like a feathery hat on Puff’s head, would be the lookout. She would point out the lost smoke-stars. Then Puff would give them a gentle nudge with his warm cinnamon-scented breath. Not too hard, not too soft. Just right.

“Like a tickle,” Wren explained, bobbing her head. “A warm guiding tickle that says, come home, little star.”

Puff nodded. A puff of cinnamon-scented air escaped his nostrils.

A tricky mission. The smoke-stars were almost invisible against the grey sky, drifting further, looking smaller and smaller. Wren darted here and there, red chest a bright speck against the white snow.

“There’s one. By the old oak tree.”

Puff carefully floated over, little dragon body glowing softly, a tiny beacon of warmth. He let out a tiny phoooof of warm air, like a soft sigh of encouragement. The smoke-star would wobble, then slowly begin to drift back toward its chimney, sometimes taking a little hesitant spiral before finding its direction.

They worked a long time, zipping and puffing through the twilight. Wren’s chirps grew a little tired. Puff’s cinnamon scent became a little fainter, like a whisper of a dream. They nudged and guided. The sun dipped low, painting the snow in soft pink and dusky purple. Stars began to peek out. Village lights twinkled below like fallen fireflies.

Then they saw it. The very last smoke-star. All alone, teetering on the very edge of the world, looking as if it might float away forever into the big vast inky night. Wren let out a small worried peep. Puff felt a little puff of nervousness in his tummy. He could see the smoke-star was about to wink out for good.

Wren fluttered her wings, gathering remaining strength.

“You can do it, Puff. Just a little bit more. You’re the warmest.”

Puff took a deep warm cinnamon-scented breath and let out his biggest gentlest puff of all. A warm hug of air, a breath full of courage and home. The smoke-star shivered, then spun around with a happy wobble and began to glide back toward its cottage. It joined the others. Suddenly the sky was not grey. Twinkling. Sparkling. Happy again, filled with a thousand tiny grateful lights.

Ever since then the village fires burned a little brighter. Wren did not announce that different friends could bring sparkle back. She only rode home on Puff’s head, tired and pleased, and if you sniff the air on a quiet night you might still catch a tiny hint of cinnamon, which is how the last star found its chimney, and how they left it.
